title: Deployment Arc choreographer: interactive storyboard for staged traffic & micro-rollback
creator: Marina Cole
description:
Summary:
Design and prototype a new 'Deployment Arc' storyboard that unifies staged traffic, temporal phasing, and micro-rollback gestures into a single interactive surface inside Redwood Console. The goal is to help operators compose and rehearse complex canaries and A/B exposures (fractional splits, cohort phasing, shadowing) while keeping rollback fast and explainable.

Problem:
Current rollout UIs are fragmentary: different pages for traffic split, canary steps, and emergency rollback. Operators repeatedly open dashboards, run external sims, and then return to the console to patch traffic rules. This creates friction during incidents and increases time-to-rollback.

Goals:
- Provide a single visual surface (storyboard) where users can author staged exposures across time and cohorts, preview traffic allocation curves, and attach safety assertions.
- Make emergency rollback a first-class, single-click action from any storyboard state with clear rationale and telemetry links.
- Surface token-cost implications of exposure trajectories so PMs and finance can decide tradeoffs during rollouts.
- Enable compact gestures for on-the-fly micro-adjustments (drag handles, nudge keys) and an undo/redo timeline.

Non-goals:
- Not shipping full multi-tenant RBAC or billing export in this ticket. Those are dependent features handled in separate ENG tickets.

Key UX concepts in prototype:
- Arc canvas: time on X, audience fraction on Y, with layered cohort lanes.
- Snapshots & playhead: capture named snapshots; scrub to see system state and expected traffic distribution at a point in time.
- Safety assertions: attach checks (error rate, latency, cost per token) with pass/fail thresholds that can pause a rollout.
- Emergency snapback: a modal with three rollback options (soft-fade, hard-snap, route-to-fallback-model) and an explainability pane summarizing metric deltas and recent traces.
- Cost overlay: live projected token spend per hour visualized on the arc. Toggle by model variant and quantization profile.
- Micro-gesture palette: drag handles for cohort curves; alt-drag for fine-grain nudges; keyboard shortcuts for ±1% and ±5% increments.
- Runbook binding: attach a short runbook or link a playbook for each snapshot so operators have immediate remediation steps.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Visual density vs. clarity: we chose a layered lane approach (less compact than stacked small-multiples) to keep rollback reasoning obvious.
- Cost inside the same surface vs. separate panel: integrated cost overlay (muted) to reduce context switches, with an expand-to-panel affordance for deeper inspection.
- Safety automation vs. manual control: prototype defaults to manual progression with optional auto-pause when an assertion fails (opt-in).

Acceptance criteria:
- Clickable Figma prototype demonstrates: authoring a three-step canary, scrubbing playhead, creating a named snapshot, and triggering emergency snapback.
- Annotated spec for component library tokens (colors, spacing, interaction states, keyboard shortcuts) delivered to devs.
- Usability test report (5 enterprise operators) with top three pain points and improvement plan.
- Handoff checklist completed: a11y checklist, performance budget for canvas rendering, telemetry hooks required for safety assertions.

Artifacts & links:
- Figma prototype: https://www.figma.com/file/EXAMPLE/deployment-arc-choreographer-proto (clickable storyboard)
- PRD in Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRD/pages/56789/Deployment+Arc+Choreographer
- Slack thread (design discussion): https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01DESIGN/p1234567890
- Engineering spike branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1429

Implementation notes for engineers (summary):
- Canvas must render up to 200 cohort lanes smoothly; recommend WebGL canvas layer for lane rendering and DOM overlay for controls.
- Telemetry hooks: exposure_start/exposure_snapshot/exposure_end events; include model_variant, cohort_id, target_fraction, timestamp, and commit_id.
- Safety assertion evaluation occurs server-side; UI polls assertion status via rollout state API.
- Cost projection is an estimated heuristic (tokens-per-minute * model-cost-per-token) surfaced as a single-line summary and an hourly curve.

Risks & mitigations:
- Misleading cost projections: clearly label as estimate and include confidence band; link to detailed cost breakdown in Console cost view.
- Operator error while composing: provide undo/redo, 'dry-run' preview, and mandatory confirm for >20% immediate shifts.
- Performance on large orgs: offload heavy sims to a sandboxed server job and show progressive results on canvas.

Next steps:
1) Run two moderated usability sessions (target: infra and product platform teams) week of 2026-03-16.
2) Iterate prototype with notes from sessions and create a trimmed 'emergency rollback' modal microflow for rapid engineering MVP.
3) Coordinate with ENG-21145 (rollout-state-api) and ENG-21146 (telemetry-contract) for integration details.
4) Prepare handoff packet and schedule dev check-in for 2026-03-25.

acceptance_criteria: Clickable Figma prototype covers authoring, snapshotting, scrubbing, and emergency snapback flow.
Design tokens and interaction spec handed off to engineering (component list + keyboard shortcuts).
Usability test report with at least 5 operator sessions and prioritized issues list.
Performance budget agreed: canvas render <200ms initial paint for up to 50 lanes; graceful degradation strategy for >100 lanes.
notes: This ticket focuses on the design and prototype. Engineering implementation will be split into an MVP (emergency rollback + basic arc authoring) and a follow-up enhancement sprint for cost projections and safety automation.
